note:
The central focus of these chapters is undoubtedly Nehemiah’s success in rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem and in securing the defenses of the city. But this is no mere construction project. It is an act of faith, sustained by prayer on the part of Nehemiah (1:5–11; 2:4; 4:4, 5; 5:19; 6:9, 14) and also of others (4:9). Such prayer is needed because of the opposition and harassment they face from surrounding peoples (2:10, 19; 4:1–14; 6:1–14). There are also internal difficulties within the community (ch. 5). But God uses Nehemiah’s leadership skills to ensure the completion of the work.

**1:1 The words of.** This introductory phrase does not settle the question as to whether the book of Nehemiah was originally composed separately from Ezra. It may indicate the beginning of personal records or memoirs by Nehemiah (see Introduction: Author).

**Nehemiah.** The name means “the LORD has comforted.”

**Chislev.** Corresponds to November/December. Unlike Ezra, who uses ordinal numerals to designate the months (e.g., Ezra 7:8, 9; 10:9, 17; but not Ezra 6:15), Nehemiah employs their Babylonian names.

**twentieth year.** If the reference is to the years of Artaxerxes's reign (which would correspond to 446 B.C.), there is a conundrum. Regnal years are customarily calculated from the month of Nisan, the first month of the year (March/April). Since 2:1 is dated clearly as occurring in March 446 B.C, 1:1 would then occur after 2:1, not before it. Obviously, Nehemiah is using some other basis for his calculation, perhaps from the month of Artaxerxes's succession (July/August). However, this proposal remains uncertain, as there are no parallel examples of such dating in other sources. Even emending the text is impossible since there are no attested textual variants, and any change would be speculative. At present, there is not enough evidence to be sure of the precise dating of these events. We know that they happened, but we just cannot presently identify exactly when. See Introduction to Ezra: Date and Occasion.

**Susa.** This city is a winter residence of the Persian kings (Esth. 1:2 note).

A short form of Hananiah, it means “the LORD is gracious.” A certain Hananiah who was head of Jewish affairs is mentioned in the Elephantine papyri and is believed by some to be the brother of Nehemiah (7:2). He and his companions may have been sent to Jerusalem as part of an official mission to survey what had happened there.

verse_quote: its gates are destroyed by fire.
note: It is less likely that this refers to the destruction 140 years earlier in the days of Nebuchadnezzar (586 B.C.). Nehemiah’s shocked reaction indicates that this is of more recent origin, most probably the result of the events recorded in Ezra 4:7–23.

Fasting is here connected with mourning (1 Sam. 31:13) as well as with making a request of God (Ezra 8:21 note). Nehemiah is a man of prayer (2:4; 4:4, 9; 5:19; 6:9, 14; 13:14, 22, 29, 31), and here he brings before God his concerns over the dismal news from Jerusalem.

**the God of heaven.** See notes on Ezra 1:2; Dan. 4:37.

In his prayer, after addressing God as supreme and the God of the covenant (v. 5), Nehemiah pleads for a response despite the sin of the people, past and present (vv. 6, 7). In vv. 8, 9 Nehemiah frames his petition on the basis of God’s word to Moses (see Deut. 7:9) and on Solomon’s temple prayer (see 2 Chr. 6:40). In addition, he mentions God’s past deliverance of the people (v. 10) before concluding with the needs of his immediate, personal situation (v. 11). From the start, Nehemiah is not concerned merely with a building project. He has in view the furtherance of God’s redemptive purposes.

**1:5** In calling on God Nehemiah captures both His transcendence and His immanence. The true God is not only far above His people as the God of heaven (v. 4 note); He is near His people as the God of the covenant (Deut. 4:7).

**who keeps covenant and steadfast love.** Nehemiah bases his petition on the constancy of God to His self-commitment, not on any merit the people possess. For “steadfast love,” see note on Ezra 7:28.
The prayer of one particular day (v. 11), after four months of prayer and fasting (1:4; 2:1 note). “Day and night” means “continually” (Josh. 1:8; Ps. 1:2).

In his intercession Nehemiah speaks in solidarity with his people (see Ezra 9:6–15). Continuing enjoyment of the blessings of the Mosaic covenant is conditioned on the obedience of the people to the Lord’s statutes. If Israel flagrantly and impenitently breaks His commands, the result is the imposition of the curses of the broken covenant. Nehemiah recognizes that Israel’s disloyalty has led to forfeiture of the covenant blessings, and the result has been exile (Ezra 9:9 note).

A common petition (Deut. 9:27; Ps. 132:1; Jer. 14:21), particularly in Nehemiah (5:19; 6:14; 13:14, 22, 29, 31). It does not imply divine forgetfulness but rather calls for God’s intervention and action based on His ongoing commitment.

The Mosaic covenant promises restoration of a remnant after exile (Deut. 30:1–5) on the basis of the covenant made with Abraham (Deut. 4:25–31). Such restoration must be accompanied by repentance and confession just as Nehemiah voices here (see Lev. 26:40–45).

**make my name dwell there.** The name of God symbolizes God Himself, as He reveals Himself to His people. A place for His name to dwell is a place for Him to be with His people and to receive their worship (Deut. 12:5 note). Though the place is unspecified in Deuteronomy, Nehemiah recognizes it as Jerusalem, in keeping with Israel’s history (see 2 Chr. 6:6).

A reference to the exodus (Ex. 32:11; Mic. 6:4). The people belong to the Lord because of His past intervention on their behalf when He saved them and claimed them for Himself. Even though they have rebelled against Him, He in His grace and forbearance has not dropped His claim on them, so His commitment can function as the basis for Nehemiah’s petition.

verse_quote: who delight to fear your name.
note:
The fear of the Lord is the proper response to God’s self-revelation. To fear God is to know Him (Prov. 9:10), trust Him (Ps. 34:11, 22), obey Him (Prov. 8:13), and show Him reverence. “Delight” shows this is far from a coerced reaction.

**this man.** Artaxerxes I.

**cupbearer.** A member of the royal court whose responsibility is to choose wine (2:1) and safeguard it from poison. As the cupbearer, Nehemiah has the complete confidence of the king. This, combined with his constant access to the king, secures for him prestige and influence at court.

The date is March/April 445 B.C.., four months after Nehemiah received the report about Jerusalem (1:1 note). Nehemiah has continued to pray for a favorable opportunity to approach the king, and on the occasion of some festivity (“wine was before him”) Artaxerxes gives an opening for him to speak.

A courtier with a sad face or anxious expression might well be implicated in a palace intrigue. Nehemiah is unaware that his prayer vigil has affected his looks.

**very much afraid.** Nehemiah fears the king’s wrath (Prov. 16:14) either because he is sad in the king’s presence, especially on a festive occasion, or because he is about to ask the king to reverse a previous decision (Ezra 4:21). Nehemiah may also fear that he will be refused the permission he seeks.
A brief, spontaneous prayer based on a life of prayer (see 1:4–11).

Rebuilding the city is one aspect of rebuilding the “house of God” (see Num. 12:7), a major theme in Ezra and Nehemiah (see Introduction to Ezra: Characteristics and Themes). It is the focus of Neh. 1:1–7:3. Though Nehemiah mentions Judah, with characteristic tact he does not name Jerusalem, which was the subject of a previous, generally negative decree of Artaxerxes (Ezra 4:21, 22).

Opinions differ as to whether this indicates the meal is held in private or whether it brings out the influence the queen might have on the king’s response.

**How long ... given him a time.** It may seem doubtful that Nehemiah requests the twelve-year absence presumed in 5:14, but his request to rebuild his personal residence (v. 8) indicates that more than brief leave is in view. No matter how long of a leave Nehemiah asks for specifically at this point, the leave is certainly extended over the years. Possibly Nehemiah makes short visits to the royal court to report to the king.

Nehemiah now makes his specific requests.

**letters.** The two references to letters in vv. 7, 8 are part of a major theme in Ezra and Nehemiah: the written word is an effective instrument used by God to accomplish His redemptive purpose (Introduction to Ezra: Characteristics and Primary Themes).

The scope of the building project becomes clear: fortress, walls, and a governor’s residence. The interval of four months has involved more than prayer. Nehemiah has been checking up on who is in charge of the king’s forest, possibly located six miles (10 km) south of Jerusalem. It is also possible that the fortress is located north of the temple to protect its most vulnerable aspect. Nehemiah has a clear idea of what will be needed.

**the good hand of my God.** Nehemiah acts as a responsible human agent in making the request, but the success is from God’s sovereign good pleasure (Ezra 7:6), a theme that expresses the overarching message of Ezra and Nehemiah (Introduction to Ezra: Characteristics and Themes).

verse_quote: The governors of the province Beyond the River.
note: In Nehemiah’s era, the chief Persian administrators are probably located in Damascus, and Nehemiah presents them with his credentials as he travels to Jerusalem. The military escort befits his status as governor of the subprovince of Judah (see Ezra 8:22).

A Babylonian name meaning “Sin [the moon god] gives life.” Sanballat and his descendants served for more than a century as the governors of Samaria, the area north of Judah. He may have worshiped the God of Israel in some fashion (2 Kin. 17:24–41), since the names of his sons, Delaiah and Shelemiah, end with a short form of “Yahweh.” “Horonite” may indicate that he came from Beth-Horon, about ten miles (16 km) northwest of Jerusalem or, less probably, from Horonaim in Moab.

**Tobiah.** Probably the governor of Ammon, east of Judah, where his family remained influential for centuries. His name means “the LORD is good,” indicating that he, too, may have worshiped the God of Israel (6:17, 18; 13:4). His son Jehohanan (6:17, 18) also had a Yahwistic name and was married to the daughter of an influential Jewish leader (3:4, 30; 6:18). Their religion was probably syncretistic.

**heard.** References to the enemies having “heard” will punctuate the rest of 1:1–7:3 like a refrain (v. 19; 4:1, 7, 15; 6:1, 16). The conflict escalates until it is resolved in 6:16.

**displeased them greatly.** The opposition has a political aspect in that Nehemiah’s presence reduces their control over Judah. But it is religious at its root (v. 20 note; Ezra 4:13 note).

Soon after returning to Jerusalem, Nehemiah conducts a nighttime inspection of the walls and, aware of God’s blessing upon him, encourages the population of the city to rebuild them.

**2:11–16** Nehemiah’s three-day wait after arriving in Jerusalem invites comparison with Ezra (Ezra 8:32). Ezra acts publicly; Nehemiah secretly (that Nehemiah has “told no one” is emphasized in v. 12; see v. 16).
A ministry of the Holy Spirit, similar to “stirred up” (Ezra 1:1, 5), except that Nehemiah consciously recognizes the divine origin of the burden he feels and the project he envisions.

Some of the damage is from Nebuchadnezzar’s day. Lack of maintenance has caused further erosion and decay of the terraces surrounding the city, perhaps at the Millo (1 Chr. 11:8 note) on the east of the city. Nehemiah has to turn back rather than circumnavigate the city, especially at night.
Much of the city has lain in ruins for almost 150 years (1:3 note). An earlier attempt to rebuild the wall was stopped (Ezra 4:7–23). Nehemiah’s presence will change all that.

verse_quote: also of the words that the king had spoken.
note:
Nehemiah’s acknowledgment of God’s sovereignty as the ultimate source of his plan does not exclude the providentially ordered actions of the king (v. 8 note).

**Let us rise up.** Nehemiah’s initiative meets with wholehearted support on the part of the leaders of Judah; by now the reader knows that this response, too, is governed by God’s purpose (Ezra 1:5 note).

Sanballat and Tobiah are well informed about what is going on in Jerusalem (see 6:17).

**Geshem the Arab.** This third opponent of Nehemiah was probably an Arab chief controlling a substantial area south of Judah, stretching to Egypt and over into Arabia. Nehemiah is pictured as virtually surrounded by enemies—Sanballat to the north, Tobiah to the east, and Geshem to the south (4:7, 8 note). The first tactic that they employed was demoralization of the people by ridiculing their proposals and insinuating that they were engaged in rebellion. Such allegations had worked a few years before (see Ezra 4:12, 13).

**2:20 God of heaven.** See note on 1:4.

**prosper.** Nehemiah has requested success from God (1:11). He associates with the people as he expresses confidence that the sovereign God will prosper their endeavors.

**you have no portion.** On this religious exclusivity, see note on Ezra 4:3. Despite their possible claims to the contrary, Nehemiah argues that their compromised religion bars them from any right to be involved in the affairs of Jerusalem.

The material of this chapter probably existed independently, perhaps as an official report, before Nehemiah incorporated it into his memoir. The chapter underscores an important theme of Ezra and Nehemiah: the people of God as a whole and not just the great leaders are vital for accomplishing God’s redemptive purpose. All of God’s people worked together to rebuild the wall: clergy and laity, craftsmen and tradesmen, by town and by family, each contributing to the completion of the whole (see Eph. 4:16).

**3:1 Eliashib.** The grandson of Jeshua, the high priest during the days of Zerubbabel.

**Sheep Gate.** The gate at the northeast corner of the city (see John 5:2) used to bring sacrificial animals into the city. That may well be why this gate is “consecrated.” The description in the following verses moves counterclockwise until the Sheep Gate is mentioned again in v. 32.

**Tower of the Hundred.** This is somewhere on the north side, the area with the poorest natural defenses.

**Tower of Hananel.** A tower on the north side.

Repeatedly in this description “next” occurs, emphasizing that Nehemiah’s allocation of work areas has been carefully planned to avoid gaps.

**the men of Jericho.** Similar groups are found in vv. 5, 7, 27. Though their own homes are elsewhere, they recognize the importance of the work going on in Jerusalem. Perhaps they are allocated sections of the wall where there are few houses.
A main gate on the north side (2 Chr. 33:14; Zeph. 1:10), this is probably the gate used by merchants (see 13:16).
Lit. “made strong.” It is possible that sections of the wall remain standing here and need only to be restored. Elsewhere it is a matter of rebuilding from the ground up.
Though the text presents an amazing picture of unanimity, it notes realistically that not all of God’s people are in harmony with what the Lord is doing through Nehemiah.
Traditionally rendered “the Old Gate,” it is on the northwest corner of the city. Possibly to be identified with the Gate of Ephraim (8:16; 12:39), which is not mentioned here.
On the west side of the northern half of the city. It probably leads off from the wall that is being repaired.
Probably others too, such as Jedaiah, work on the sections near their homes.
On the west side of the city, perhaps at the midpoint.
An extraordinary testimony to the dedication of the whole community to the task of rebuilding (5:1 note; 12:43 note).

On the west side of the city facing the Tyropean Valley.

**a thousand cubits.** About five hundred yards (457 m). A substantial length of wall, perhaps less seriously damaged or repaired earlier.

**Dung Gate.** On the southwest corner of the city facing the Hinnom Valley.

On the southeast corner of the city facing the Kidron Valley.

**city of David.** Though in disrepair, it is still the city David established to be the political and religious capital of the theocracy. There is continuity between the past and present generations (Ezra 2:1–70 note).
On either side of the high priest’s house the work is done by Levites (vv. 17–19) and priests (vv. 20–22). Meremoth (v. 21) is mentioned in the list of priests in 10:5, as is Baruch (v. 20) in 10:6.

Nehemiah charges each individual to repair the section of the wall in which that individual and his family takes the most interest. This fosters personal motivation that will help get the job done (see 3:28–30).

Usually located south of the temple mount, but more probably it also includes the southern part of the city below the Water Gate.

**Water Gate.** About halfway up the east side of the city, this gate faces the Kidron Valley and the main water source, the Gihon Spring.
On the northeast side of the city.
Just north of the Horse Gate.
Between the East Gate and the Sheep Gate.
The counterclockwise description has come full circle (v. 1 note).
Nehemiah’s comprehensive program of work in ch. 3 conveys a sense of orderly progress. The reality is otherwise. No sooner has the work started than the opposition to it escalates.

Sanballat is evidently the leading figure in the confrontation. “His brothers” are his allies. His series of questions claim that the Jews have underestimated what they can do and have started something they will be unable to complete. At the same time, he knows that his mockery will be reported in Jerusalem and will erode confidence in the project.
He appears in a subordinate role, echoing Sanballat. A fox weighs only a few pounds, but Tobiah alleges its weight to be sufficient to topple any wall the Jews contrive to build.

This is the first of three such imprecatory prayers uttered by Nehemiah (6:14; 13:29). An imprecatory prayer is one that calls for the enemy to experience God’s curse (e.g., Pss. 79:12; 94:1–3; 137:7–9). See Introduction to Psalms: Special Issues. These individuals are in reality opposing the work of God, and it is from Him that Nehemiah seeks redress. At the same time, neither he nor the people give up their work rebuilding the wall., 5

One more group, the Ashdodites, is added to the list of enemies. Nehemiah is now completely encircled by the enemy. Ashdod, a city in the Philistine plain to his west (2:19 note), is also the name of a Persian subprovince corresponding to Philistine territory.
The people respond as Nehemiah has done. Corporate prayer is accompanied by common-sense precautions: “set a guard.”

A collective term is used, emphasizing that discouragement is widespread.

**The strength ... the wall.** Perhaps this poetic couplet is chanted by the people. Part of the reason they are discouraged is simply that the work is hard.
Their adversaries plan to spring an unexpected attack on Jerusalem, but it is abandoned (v. 15), seemingly because information about it leaks out, and the element of surprise is lost.

Ten is a symbolic number for completeness. The fear of violence is growing in the minds of the people. It seems that Jews who live near Israel and Ammon have become aware of the intention to attack Jerusalem. However, they add to the tension in the city by repeatedly urging those at work there to abandon the capital and scatter throughout Judea.

Nehemiah has no thought of fleeing before an impending attack. His first action is to station additional guards at the most vulnerable points. The tension continues to rise as the people of Judah take up arms for the first time.

See theological note “The Incomprehensibility of God” on p. 630. Nehemiah not only arms the people physically; he also bolsters them spiritually by reminding them of the Lord (“Adonai,” the sovereign Lord) who supports them.

In Ezra 4:5, 24 the enemy frustrated the plan to build the temple; here God responds in kind by frustrating the plan to stop building the wall. A surprise invasion is no longer possible, and any attack will be stoutly resisted.

**we all returned to the wall.** Nehemiah responds successfully to the tide of discouragement by adding guards and exhorting the people.
The arms first mentioned in v. 13 are supplemented here with shield and armor (a breastplate of metal). The immediate threat has waned, but Nehemiah wisely maintains a state of readiness.

verse_quote: Those who carried ... held his weapon.
note: The porters have a hand free to hold a weapon, which may have be no more than a stone for throwing.

verse_quote: each of the builders had his sword.
note:
The builders need two hands to work, so they wear swords at their sides.

**the trumpet.** The trumpet, or _shofar_, has numerous functions in the OT. Here, as in Judg. 3:27, it rallies the troops.

verse_quote: Our God will fight for us.
note: The Lord has intervened on behalf of His people who are acting in accordance with His wishes (see Ex. 14:14; Josh. 10:14).
Shows how strong their dedication is, since work usually ends at sundown in this era.
A picture of constant readiness to respond to any attack.

This section leaves the main topic of opposition by outsiders to consider the difficulties that have arisen from within. Probable causes of the economic stress mentioned are that Judah has been cut off from trading with neighbors; farmers are away from their fields because they have stayed in Jerusalem (4:22); there is a famine (v. 3); and previous administrators have burdened the people (v. 15). Times are so bad that children are being sold into slavery, houses and vineyards are being mortgaged, and money is being borrowed at interest. The crushing realization for Nehemiah is that the people of God themselves are forcing these intolerable measures on each other, not foreigners. It is improbable that these conditions have originated within the fifty-two days it has taken to rebuild the wall. That project, however, has intensified the stress and brought it out into the open. It is a serious threat to completion of the work.

**5:1 their wives.** Since women play a minor role in Ezra and Nehemiah, mentioning them here emphasizes the severity of the crisis (3:12 note; 12:43 note).
Famines are often signs of God’s judgment (Deut. 11:16, 17; 1 Chr. 21:12; Hag. 1:7–11). Perhaps this famine is God’s judgment upon the leaders’ failure to do what is right.
A property tax that they cannot pay except by mortgaging their property to raise funds.

According to Lev. 25:39–43, a man in the old covenant community who becomes poor can sell himself, along with his family, to a fellow Israelite in order to get back on his feet financially; he has to be treated as a hired worker, not as a slave. The error in Nehemiah’s day seems to be twofold: (a) only the children are being sold, resulting in the breakup of family units; (b) the children are being treated as slaves, not as hired workers.

Despite his indignation at what is happening, Nehemiah does not act precipitately but thinks through an appropriate reaction.

**brought charges against.** A bold step on Nehemiah’s part.

**exacting interest.** The law prohibits not only usury but interest of any kind (Ex. 22:25–27; Lev. 25:35–37; Deut. 23:20).

Earlier Nehemiah’s administration was buying out of slavery Jews held as slaves in surrounding nations, some perhaps from the days of Nebuchadnezzar. More recently, however, they have been redeeming Jews sold as slaves by their fellow countrymen because they of their inability to repay debts.
Their public conduct should enhance the religion they professed.

Views differ as to what Nehemiah says regarding his own conduct. He, along with his family, may be making interest-bearing loans to encourage the people to repent and change their behavior. In the light of his reaction in v. 6, it is more probable that he is extending interest-free loans of money and grain, and exhorting others to follow his personal example.

While some take the rate of interest charged as one percent per month, that would be exceptionally low for the Persian Empire, where forty or fifty percent annual interest was common. Here the expression does not specify the rate.

**grain, wine, and oil.** This familiar triad is in the order of the agricultural harvests: first grain, then grapes, and finally olives ripened.

Nehemiah characteristically takes immediate action, which shrewdly limits any propensity to forget the agreement that has been made. This oath is a renewal of their commitment to keep the law of Moses concerning lending and debt slavery. See theological note “Oaths and Vows” on previous page.

In this covenant renewal Nehemiah dramatizes the curses for failing to keep the oath (see Jer. 34:8–22). Any who fail to keep his commitment will be shaken loose from his property as easily as the fold in Nehemiah’s cloak could be straightened out.

This retrospective reflection on his governorship is probably composed by Nehemiah and inserted by him at a later date because it clarifies the nature of his personal conduct while in office.

**5:14 twentieth year ... thirty-second year.** This twelve-year period (445 B.C. to 433 B.C.) is Nehemiah’s first term as governor; afterward he is recalled to the Persian court (13:6, 7), but subsequently he returns to Jerusalem for a second term of unknown length.

**the food allowance of the governor.** A governor has the right to collect taxes for his personal support. Nehemiah waives this right for the benefit of the people (v. 18; see 1 Cor. 9:4, 12; 2 Thess. 3:8, 9).

Sheshbazzar (Ezra 5:14) and Zerubbabel (Hag. 1:1) were former governors, but their terms were almost one hundred years earlier. The oppressive governors were Nehemiah’s more immediate predecessors, whose policies were harmful to the people (5:1–13 note).

**fear of God.** See notes on 1:11 and v. 9, where we see how Nehemiah urged others to act from the same motive.

Nehemiah’s reason for being governor is service, not personal advancement, corresponding to his reason for going to Judah in the first place (2:5). He does not use the misfortune of the people to acquire land and amass a fortune for himself.
According to Persian custom, Nehemiah as governor has to entertain the officials under his authority as well as visiting dignitaries from other countries.

The food listed can feed hundreds of people. Nehemiah is as generous as he is rich. By not demanding all that he might rightfully demand, he reveals that he is acting out of compassion for the heavily burdened people.

The second use of “remember” in a prayer (1:8 note) and the first of four prayers asking God to “remember me” (13:14, 22, 31). This is not a claim of merit before God but evidence of his faith, which relies on God’s promises.

After the digression in ch. 5 from the main theme of rebuilding the wall, the main narrative continues. The conflict that had been steadily escalating reaches its climax, when the wall was virtually complete. This final attempt to stop the work was threefold: to harm (vv. 2–4), to frighten (vv. 5–9), and to discredit (vv. 10–13) Nehemiah.

**6:1 when Sanballat ... heard.** The phrase continues the series of similar phrases (2:10 note) and brings the reader back to the main topic of Neh. 1:1–7:3.

In the northwestern corner of Judah, as far from the safety of Jerusalem as possible without leaving the country.

**to do me harm.** A vague phrase, perhaps referring to murder (v. 10) or to a later allegation that Nehemiah’s trip to Ono is to enlist others in revolt against Persia (v. 6).
Nehemiah sees that the basic purpose of the plot is to halt the work on the wall. His diplomatically worded response embodies a determined refusal.
Both sides are persistent as the conflict reaches its climax. Nehemiah’s opponents are obviously desperate.
Letters are normally sealed, but Sanballat wants this letter to be public so as to sway public opinion against continuing with the work.

The accusation is plausible: the wall is being rebuilt, Judah has a history of rebellion against her overlords, and Nehemiah is a skillful leader with a passion for his homeland. The “nations” are the surrounding provinces of the Persian Empire., 7
Nehemiah robustly rebuts the allegations.

A figure denoting discouragement (see Ezra 4:4), here as a result of the campaign of psychological harassment.

**now ... strengthen my hands.** Another of the brief prayers so characteristic of Nehemiah (1:4 note).

Otherwise unknown. As well as being a prophet (v. 12), he may also be a priest, giving him access to the temple.

**who was confined to his home.** It may have been under pretext of illness or as a symbolic action denoting the need to seek a secure refuge. Up to this point Nehemiah seems to have no suspicions regarding Shemaiah.

**in the house of God.** The final ploy now unfolds. Nehemiah might seek asylum in the courtyard of the temple (Ex. 21:12–14), but he is not allowed to enter the temple itself since he is not a priest (Num. 18:7).
Nehemiah’s courage shines through again (5:7 note).
Since the action Shemaiah proposes is contrary to God’s Word, this exposes him as a false prophet (see Deut. 13:1–5; Is. 8:19, 20).

verse_quote: I should be afraid ... taunt me.
note: The idea is to make Nehemiah behave like a coward and a lawbreaker, so that his reputation will be ruined and he will lack support to finish the wall.

The third use of “remember” in a prayer (1:8 note) and the second imprecatory prayer (4:4, 5 note), as the “remembering” here is unto judgment.

**Noadiah and the rest of the prophets.** False prophecy was prevalent in Jerusalem before the exile (see Jer. 23:9–32; Ezek. 13). There are evidently influential figures in the city who are in league with Nehemiah’s opponents.

Although opposition to rebuilding the walls ceases with their completion (v. 16), attempts to intimidate Nehemiah continue (6:17–19). Nehemiah takes measures to secure the gates of the city against possible continuing aggression by Israel’s enemies (7:1–3).

**6:15 So the wall was finished.** A transitional verse that concludes the section that began in v. 1 and opens the final episode of Neh. 1:1–7:3. The last of six attempts to stop the work failed.

**the twenty-fifth day of ... Elul.** October 2, 445 B.C. , though this is sometimes disputed as being too late since Elul normally occurs in August/September.

**fifty-two days.** A speedy outcome, the result of effective leadership. Based on the aforementioned October completion date, the work must have begun on August 12.

The peoples encircling Judah will no longer be able to dominate and exploit the community as they have been doing.

**with the help of our God.** Nehemiah disclaims any personal congratulation in the matter and points to the decisive factor in their achievement.

Tobiah’s relation by marriage to those at work on the wall provides a natural channel for the transfer of information about the circumstances in Jerusalem to Nehemiah’s opponents.

**the nobles of Judah.** They are evidently sympathetic to Tobiah and constitute an influential source of opposition to Nehemiah.
May refer to trading arrangements rather than connections by marriage.

This demonstrates that the wall is now complete (6:1).

**the gatekeepers, the singers, and the Levites.** These temple officials seem to be mentioned in connection with the security of the wall, presumably because that is key to the security of the temple itself.

Leaders are appointed to oversee the security of the city.

**Hananiah.** See note on 1:2.

**God-fearing.** See note on 1:11. Hananiah’s faithful discharge of his duties is grounded in his deep spiritual commitment.

Guards are appointed to secure the gates at night. The gates are usually opened at dawn; waiting until later (when the sun has been up long enough to make things really warm) is a security measure for the city.

The second major section of the book (7:4–13:30) begins with a record of how Nehemiah prepares to meet the need to repopulate Jerusalem (vv. 4, 5) by consulting a genealogical record of exiles who returned earlier (vv. 5–73). This is substantially similar to Ezra 2:3–60.

**7:4 no houses had been rebuilt.** More probably, “were being rebuilt.” There are occupied houses in Jerusalem at this time (see 3:10, 20, 23, 24, 29). The problem is the sparse population and the lack of enthusiasm for residing in the city. People are content to dwell in the agricultural hinterland.

verse_quote: my God put it into my heart.
note:
See note on 2:8. Nehemiah is aware of divine leading on the matter (2:12).

**enrolled by genealogy.** The purpose of this registration is to help repopulate Jerusalem, as will become clear when this topic is resumed in 11:1, 2. Nehemiah wants the city populated by people of demonstrably Jewish descent, a faithful remnant of the covenant people.

**book of the genealogy ... at the first.** On the theological significance of this list, see note on Ezra 2:1–70. The repetition of the list underscores the continuity of Nehemiah’s generation with the first ones to return.

verse_quote: a priest with Urim and Thummim.
note: A recognized method of discerning God’s will (see Ezra 2:63).

The covenant community is rebuilt as Israel renews its covenant with God (7:73–10:39), dedicates the walls of the city (chs. 11; 12), and obeys other aspects of the law (ch. 13).

**7:73–10:39** This section is often viewed as intrusive in the flow of the narrative. Why not move straight from the completion of the city walls (6:15) to their dedication (chs. 11; 12)? The likely answer is that it is inappropriate to dedicate the walls before there are sufficient inhabitants in Jerusalem to constitute a functioning city.

**7:73 when the seventh month had come.** As Nehemiah characteristically names a month (see 1:1 note), this numerical designation (see 8:2) points to with this section’s being drawn from another source, as does the impersonal, third-person style. It is often argued that it has been taken from Ezra’s memoir. The date corresponds to October 8, 445 B.C., just six days after the completion of the wall (6:15).

verse_quote: the square before the Water Gate.
note:
Located on the east side of Jerusalem. Open plazas were frequently situated within the walls at the entrances of ancient cities.

**they told Ezra.** Ezra’s ministry began thirteen years earlier. Some of its fruit is now evident in that the people, who have gathered with united purpose, call for the Book of the Law to learn more from it. It is not known where Ezra has been in the intervening period. Possibly his official duties required him to return to the royal court, only traveling back to Jerusalem with Nehemiah. Alternatively he may have stayed in Jerusalem in a private capacity as he continued his teaching ministry.

The participants, including women and children capable of understanding what is going on (repeated in v. 3), are in keeping with those required to be present at the reading of the law prescribed for the Feast of Booths in Deut. 31:10–13.

**first day of the seventh month.** This is the start of the civil year and the time for celebrating the Feast of Trumpets (Num. 29:1–6).

verse_quote: he read from it facing the square.
note: For the public reading of the law in the context of covenant ratification or renewal, see Ex. 24:7; Josh. 8:30–35; 2 Kin. 23:1–3. The reading (along with the exposition, vv. 7, 8) takes five or six hours.

A scroll; the codex or book form did not yet exist in Nehemiah’s day.

**all the people stood.** By standing they express their reverence for the law (see v. 6).

The people concur in the praise offered by Ezra; the repetition expresses the emphatic degree of assent.

**lifting up their hands.** Lifting the hands often accompanies prayer and praise to God in this era (Pss. 28:2; 63:4; 134:2; 1 Tim. 2:8).

The law is not only read but also explained to ensure that the people grasp the meaning. There may also have been translation from Hebrew to Aramaic. The doctrine of the perspicuity (clarity) of Scripture is that the things necessary for salvation can be understood from the Bible without special techniques or higher education. This truth does not eliminate the need for faithful exposition of the Scriptures by trained people (Ezra 7:6–10).

There is unity among all the leaders on this occasion. Contrary to some scholarship, the text clearly affirms that Nehemiah and Ezra are contemporaries.

**This day is holy ... do not mourn.** Holiness and mourning are not mutually exclusive (Lev. 23:26–32; Is. 6:3–5), but on this occasion sorrow is inappropriate. After the people renew their grasp of the message of the truth (v. 8), they are emotionally affected and mourn because they are filled with remorse over past sin. This then leads into renewed obedience to the truth (vv. 13–18).

Those who have plenty to eat are to share with those who do not (see Ps. 22:26). This incident provides an illustration for understanding the sin in 1 Cor. 11:17–34.

**the joy of the** LORD**.** The people rejoice in the salvation and blessing that the Lord has extended to them. Continuing cheerful acknowledgment of their dependence on Him will be an ongoing source of strength to the community as the Lord blesses their commitment.
“Understanding” (see vv. 7, 8) is a major theme in the passage, as is the involvement of “the people” (the term occurs thirteen times in vv. 1–12).
The smaller group has responsibility for directing others. Recognizing their need to have a thorough grounding in the truth, they seek further education, while the majority of the people go home.

This temporary living arrangement is a reminder of life in the wilderness after the redemption from Egypt and before entering the Promised Land (Lev. 23:42, 43). It is a festival that involves the whole family.

**the feast of the seventh month.** The Feast of Booths (Lev. 23:34–40), celebrated for seven days from the fifteenth to the twenty-first of the month, followed by an eighth day of solemn assembly on the twenty-second of the month (October 22–28, 445 B.C.., plus October 29). As the meeting for study of the Scriptures occurs on the second of the month, there is sufficient time for preparations to be made.
On the northwest of the city (see 3:6) but, like the Water Gate, close to the temple precincts.

Although the Feast of Booths was celebrated earlier (see Ezra 3:4), the people did not fulfill the requirement to camp out, a memorial of the time spent in the wilderness of Sinai (cf. Lev. 23:42, 43). Through study of the Scripture, neglect of this element is remedied in a way that has not occurred since the days of Joshua.
Throughout the feast, reading from the Pentateuch is assigned an important role.

verse_quote: the twenty-fourth day of this month.
note:
October 31, 445 B.C.. There is an interval of only one day before this further solemn assembly. The acts of humiliation and fasting resume after a period of postponement (8:9–18) because there has been no opportunity to express such corporate repentance.

**were assembled.** In 8:1 the people gathered to hear the law; here they gather to confess their sins in response to it (v. 3).
Covenant transgression can be confessed only by the covenant people. See note on Ezra 9:7.
LORD**.** It is read for about three hours, and then a further three hours are spent on responding appropriately in confession and worship.
These may give access to the platform (8:4), or they may lead up to the temple.

In this prayer of praise, the Levites (vv. 4, 5) address God on behalf of the people, extolling Him as creator (v. 6) and redeemer (vv. 7–12), lawgiver and disciplinarian, savior and judge (vv. 13–31). On the basis of His character and covenant, they petition God to take notice of their distress (vv. 32–37) in preparation for their covenant renewal (9:38–10:39 and note). The sequence of 9:5–10:39 resembles the form of ancient covenants: preamble identifying the overlord (vv. 5, 6), historical prologue (vv. 7–37), acceptance of the covenant (9:38–10:29), and covenant stipulations (10:30–39).
The Septuagint inserts “And Ezra said” (text note). Whether the prayer is uttered collectively by the Levites or by Ezra, its theology reflects his instruction over the preceding decade.

The people praise God for choosing Abraham and giving him the covenant of promise (Gen. 12–22).

**9:8 made with him the covenant.** This covenant with Abraham (Gen. 15) is the basis upon which God’s grace is extended time and again to His unfaithful people, as is brought out in the remainder of this prayer of praise.

**you have kept your promise.** God’s promise to Abraham was conditioned only upon God’s righteous oath (Gen. 15:9–21; Deut. 9:4–6; Heb. 6:13–18).
God is praised for redeeming Israel from Egypt (Ex. 1–19).

The praise of God continues with an account of the giving of the law at Mount Sinai and God’s gracious provisions in the wilderness.

**9:13 Mount Sinai.** See Ex. 20.

**right rules ... good statutes.** The law is perceived not as a burden but as a delight (Ps. 119:5–16; Rom. 7:12).
The Sabbath is a key symbol in the law (Is. 56:2, 4, 6; Ezek. 20:13, 16, 21, 24; 22:8; 23:38).
A reference to God’s oath to Abraham (Ex. 6:8).

The first confession of sin.

**stiffened their neck** (also in v. 29). A metaphor drawn from a stubborn animal that refuses to lower its neck to receive a yoke. This metaphor shows that the people acted with defiance toward God and their covenant commitments.

**9:17 appointed a leader.** See Num. 14:1–4. In contrast to the unfaithfulness of Israel is the faithfulness of God to His oath to Abraham (vv. 8, 15; Ezra 9:13 note).
God’s grace shines all the more brightly when juxtaposed against Israel’s sin (Rom. 9:22–24).
God’s continual care in the wilderness was due not to Israel’s obedience but to His compassion, stemming from His promise to Abraham (vv. 7, 8).
God enabled the Israelites to conquer the land of Canaan in keeping with His promise to Abraham (vv. 7, 8).
Cavities in the rock used to store water from the rainy season.
Israel responded to God’s faithfulness with disobedient rebellion during the days of the judges. For the pattern of rebellion, oppression, petition, and salvation, see Judg. 2:10–19.
Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more (Rom. 5:20).

The praise of God continues with mention of His patience during the monarchy.

**9:29 he shall live by them.** The Mosaic covenant offered life for obedience (Lev. 18:5; Rom. 10:5). Israel’s failure to merit life in the land testifies to the universal need for a substitute through whom the righteous requirements of the law are fully met (Rom. 8:3, 4).

In the Hebrew text, this word is last in the verse; it occurs also at the beginning of the prayer in v. 6, marking vv. 6–31 as unit. At this point in the prayer, the celebration of God’s faithfulness in history gives way to a petition for similar divine action in the present.

The petition is that God will do again what He did in the past: see the distress of His people and come to their aid.

**kings of Assyria.** These are the Neo-Assyrian kings whose presence was felt in Syria-Palestine from c. 850 B.C.., culminating the attack of Tiglath-pileser III (Pul) on Israel (2 Kin. 15:19), which led to the overthrow of the northern kingdom. Afterward came the Neo-Babylonian kings in the late seventh century and then the Persian kings in the mid-sixth century.
The execution of the covenant curses throughout Israel’s history was in perfect harmony with the principle of divine justice, which lay at the foundation of the Mosaic covenant (Ezra 9:9 note).
The leaders are singled out as particularly responsible., 35

See note on Ezra 9:9. Neither Ezra nor Nehemiah as representatives of the Persian regime is seeking to incite rebellion. The existing state of the people cannot, however, be what was envisioned in the original covenant promises.
Implicit in this statement is a request for aid (v. 32 note).

The people not only pray for aid but also renew their obligations under the Mosaic covenant. From the beginning, the Mosaic covenant had to be renewed after periods of covenant violation (Ex. 34; 1 Sam. 12; 2 Kin. 23).

**9:38 a firm covenant in writing.** Not the usual word for covenant but one that emphasizes the obligatory aspect of a solemn agreement. When the law is written down and sealed, it can become an effective instrument in the redemptive purposes of God (see Introduction to Ezra: Characteristics and Primary Themes).

The leaders who renewed the covenant are listed. Surprisingly Ezra is absent, being treated as a member of the priestly family of Seriah (10:2; see Ezra 7:1). Ezra played a significant role in ch. 8 but has now quietly disappeared from the scene. His job was successfully completed when the people themselves could read from the law and understand it on their own.

**10:1 On the seals are the names.** This list of eighty-four names, about half of whom are not mentioned elsewhere, reinforces one of the major themes of Ezra and Nehemiah: the people of God as a whole, not just the great leaders, are vital for the accomplishing of God’s redemptive plan (see Introduction to Ezra: Characteristics and Themes). Nehemiah and Zedekiah are joined together as representing the civil power. Many of the priestly names are those of families rather than individuals.

The whole community (vv. 28, 29) pledges fidelity to the terms of the covenant, specifically identifying and applying those parts of the Mosaic ordinances that are under the most severe pressure in their contemporary circumstances (vv. 30–39).

**10:28 all who have separated themselves.** See Ezra 6:21. This renunciation of heathen practices may additionally point in this context to those who acted on the issue of intermarriage (Ezra 9; 10).

The swearing of the oath by the people (9:15; Ezra 10:5 note) emphasizes the distinctively legal nature of the Mosaic covenantal arrangement as compared to the Abrahamic covenant in which the oath is taken by God alone (Gen. 12:1–3; 15; Heb. 6:13–18). As the apostle Paul later reveals, the Mosaic law was a kind of “guardian” that did not annul the covenant of promise already made with Abraham (Gal. 3:17, 24). Throughout the history of redemption, all God’s covenantal arrangements call for obedience springing from faith in God and willingness to observe the terms of the covenant. This is true even for the Abrahamic covenant, wherein reception of its blessings required faith that bore fruit in obedience. However, under none of God’s covenants with Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, and the new covenant church are people saved by their works of obedience. Justification is always and only by faith in the Lord’s promises (Rom. 4:1–12).

**a curse.** Covenant ratification involves a self-maledictory ceremony in which subscribers acknowledge the penalties that will be imposed on any who violate the covenant’s terms and invoke such penalties on themselves if they act unfaithfully (see Deut. 28:15–68; Jer. 34:18).

Particular pledges of obedience are elaborated. (1) The avoidance of intermarriage (v. 30; see Ezra 9:2). (2) Keeping the Sabbath and the sabbatical year (v. 31; Ex. 20:8–11; Lev. 25:1–7). (3) Support for the service of the temple (vv. 32, 33). In Ex. 30:11–16 the levy is a half-shekel, but there it seems to be a particular, rather than an annual, levy. Alternatively, the difference could be from the use of a new monetary system under the Persians, or it could be a concession to the hard economic times. (4) Provision of wood for the fire on the altar (v. 34), not specifically required previously. (5) Donation of the firstfruits (vv. 35–37; Num. 18:12, 13; Deut. 26:1–11). (6) Payment of tithes (vv. 37, 38; see Lev. 27:30; Num. 18:21–24). (7) The Levites additionally tithe the tithes they receive for the temple service (vv. 38, 39).

verse_quote: not neglect the house of our God.
note: The pledge to maintain the temple and its services as specified in the preceding verses is an index of the renewed spiritual commitment of the people. Rebuilding the house of God is a major theme in Ezra and Nehemiah (see Introduction to Ezra: Characteristics and Primary Themes).

Apart from the chief men of the nation and temple personnel, few people were settled in Jerusalem at the completion of the wall repair because the ruined state of Jerusalem discouraged settlement there (7:4). A balanced community, however, requires a wider spread of population, and the repair of the wall and gates has made it less of a hardship to reside there. Having just renewed the covenant, the people decide to “tithe” out of their own number as a holy gift to ensure the functioning of the “holy city” (vv. 1, 18).

**11:1 cast lots.** This phrase ties this list to the pledges in 10:30–39 (see 10:34) and shows the quick implementation of those pledges.

**one out of ten.** Populating the city by means of a tenth of the people is the first step in not neglecting the house of God, as pledged in 10:39.

**the holy city.** A rare phrase, used elsewhere only in v. 18; Is. 48:2; 52:1. Holiness has been expanding—from holy vessels (Ezra 1:7; see 8:28) to priests (Ezra 8:28), to people (Ezra 9:2), to the holy place (Ezra 9:8), to the gates (3:1), and to the Sabbaths (9:14). The entire city is now holy, dedicated to the service of the Lord.
It is uncertain whether this refers to a second group in addition to the tenth chosen by lot or to the willing spirit displayed by those who were chosen.
Paralleled in 1 Chr. 9:2–22, where mention is also made of representatives of tribes other than Judah, Benjamin, and Levi.
See note on Ezra 1:5.

Because it is difficult to relate this appointment to those in 3:9, 12, or 7:2, some have supposed that “second” relates to the Second Quarter of the city (see 2 Kin. 22:14), a residential area on the western hill; however, archaeologists are uncertain if that area was occupied at this juncture.

Priests (vv. 10–14), Levites (vv. 15–18), and gatekeepers (v. 19) are all resident in Jerusalem after the wall is repaired. The same priestly lines are referred to in 1 Chr. 9:10–13, with some names variously spelled. The total of 1,192 priests in Nehemiah differs from the 1,760 of 1 Chr. 9:13, but the reasons for this are unclear. There are also unexplained differences regarding the Levite family leaders compared to 1 Chr. 9:14–16 and regarding the gatekeepers (1 Chr. 9:17–22).
The ridge south of the temple.
The reference may be to David (12:24; 1 Chr. 25) or to King Artaxerxes (Ezra 7:21–24), the latter being more likely because of the information given in v. 24.

A list of those who resettled the area surrounding Jerusalem. It links with Ezra 2:21–35, binding Ezra and Nehemiah into a whole. The list is not comprehensive but points to the extent of settlement in Judah. Cf. Josh. 15.

These lists of priests and Levites who serve in the Jerusalem temple during the Persian period may make for challenging reading, but they are a significant part of the picture being presented: legitimacy through continuity. The priestly offices are hereditary, and genealogical lists establish the validity of contemporary incumbents in the postexilic period. The restored community wants to ensure that every aspect of its worship corresponds to what God desires.

**12:1–9** This list of priests (vv. 1–7) and Levites (vv. 8, 9) who returned under Zerubbabel connects the end of Nehemiah to the beginning of Ezra, uniting the whole work. In total twenty-two chiefs (leaders) of the priests are listed, whereas David appointed twenty-four priestly divisions (1 Chr. 24:7–19). Perhaps two lines died out during the exile.

**12:1 Zerubbabel ... Jeshua.** See note on Ezra 2:2.

**Ezra.** Not the same Ezra as the leading figure of Ezra and Nehemiah. That Ezra returned eighty years after Zerubbabel (Ezra 7:6 note).
For antiphonal singing, see v. 24.
Gives the high-priestly line. Eliashib is high priest in Nehemiah’s day (see 3:1). Scholars dispute whether the line is continued to the time of Darius II or Darius III (see v. 22).
This list is repeated with certain variations from vv. 1–7. The name Hattush (v. 2) is omitted, and there are a number of spelling differences.

A list of heads of Levitical families.

**12:22 Darius the Persian.** May be Darius II (423–404 B.C.) or Darius III (336–331). According to the first-century historian Josephus, Jaddua was high priest at the time of Alexander the Great (around 330 B.C.), which would support the latter identification. However, the Jaddua mentioned by Josephus need not be the one intended here. Moreover, Josephus often proves unreliable in his discussion of the Persian period.
Probably an official temple record (see Ezra 4:15).
Makes clear that the arrangements are divinely sanctioned. Persian kings were ordinarily interested in ordering the affairs of temples according to local custom.

The temple itself was dedicated earlier (Ezra 6:16). This ceremony is for the completed wall surrounding God’s “house” (the temple as such and the community). In this section Nehemiah writes in the first person (vv. 31, 38, 40). Apart from 12:44–47 where third-person references to Nehemiah recur, the remainder of the book is drawn from his memoirs.

**12:27 sought the Levites.** The dedication could not take place without the help of the Levites, who are included in the preceding lists (vv. 1–26) and now live outside Jerusalem. The significance of the event is obvious to those making the careful arrangements for it.
Hence the list in 11:22, 23., 29

Ritual purification is a representation or symbol of moral purity (Lev. 16:30).

**12:31–39** A grand procession takes place, apparently beginning at the Valley Gate on the western wall (3:13). Part of the procession, led by Ezra (v. 36), moves counterclockwise (v. 31), passing the Dung Gate, the Fountain Gate, and the Water Gate before proceeding to the temple. The other part of the procession, accompanied by Nehemiah (v. 38), moves clockwise (v. 38), passing the gates on the north side of the city before going to the temple. For the locations, see ch. 3 and notes.
A visible demonstration of what has been achieved and evidence that the walls are sturdily built. These groups weigh much more than a fox (see 4:3). 38

verse_quote: Ezra the scribe went before them.
note: Because of his priestly descent, Ezra is qualified to lead the choir, whereas Nehemiah as a lay official follows (v. 38).

The people rejoice because God has given them cause to do so by His sovereign work through human agents (see Introduction to Ezra: Characteristics and Primary Themes). It is an echo of the joy experienced ninety years before when the temple foundations were laid (Ezra 3:13). This time, however, there is no weeping.

**the women and children.** Including women and children underlines the great size of the celebration (3:12 note; 5:1 note).

These verses show that the people honored their pledge (10:39) and not neglected the house of God after the excitement of the day of celebration was over. Possibly “the days of Nehemiah” (v. 47) indicates this was added later to Nehemiah’s memoir.

**12:44 storerooms.** They adjoin the main temple building to the north and south.

verse_quote: command of David and his son Solomon.
note: See 1 Chr. 25; 2 Chr. 8:14.
The people of God as a whole, not just the great leaders, are vital for accomplishing God’s redemptive plan.

These further excerpts from Nehemiah’s memoirs relate to his second period as governor (see v. 6). He was recalled to the Persian court in 433 B.C. (5:14 note). His return may reasonably be dated after 430 B.C.. and certainly before Artaxerxes’ death in 424 B.C.. How long he remained governor is unknown. It is known that another individual became governor of the Persian subprovince of Yehud (Judah) before 407 B.C. On his return Nehemiah quickly realizes that in his relatively brief absence, the conduct of the people has deteriorated considerably and that he must take stern measures to maintain the spiritual strength of the community.

**13:1–3** The pledge of general obedience to the law of Moses (10:28, 29) includes separation from neighboring peoples (10:28). Deut. 23:3–6 requires the exclusion of any Ammonite or Moabite from an assembly of the people for worshiping the Lord. However, the people have not conformed to this aspect of the law even though the exclusion of “those of foreign descent” is in keeping with the pledge in 10:28, 29. In view is religious, not racial or political, separation (Ezra 4:3 note). It probably does not include those who have professed allegiance to the Lord. Members of the nations excluded from the assembly of Israel could be included if they put their faith in Yahweh, the covenant Lord of Israel and only true God. Ruth the Moabite, ancestor of both David and Christ, is a prominent example of this reality (Ruth 1:1–18; 4; Matt. 1:1–17).

**13:1 On that day.** The reference may well be to a celebration of the Feast of Booths in a sabbatical year when the law is read to all the people (Deut. 31:9–13). The chronological references in vv. 4, 6 make clear that it is after Nehemiah’s first term as governor, but it is unclear how the incident relates to his second term of office.
The story of Balaam is found in Num. 22–24.
Though Ezra is not on the scene, his labor is still bearing fruit (10:1–27 note). Once more (see 8:13–18), hearing the Word of God leads to renewed obedience, the obedience of separation.

The final commitment not to neglect the house of God (10:39) was violated during Nehemiah’s absence (v. 11), as were the commandments governing both the pledges for the storehouse and the tithes (10:37–39). Reform is needed upon Nehemiah’s return.

**13:4 Eliashib.** Though this Eliashib is possibly the high priest (3:1 note), it is more likely that another priest with the same name is intended, since the high priest is not likely to be placed in charge of the storehouse.

**Tobiah.** See note on 2:10. He is well connected with the Jerusalem upper classes, having himself married into one of them, while his son marries into another. He is a daring and persistent character who attracts significant supporters.
It is because of a lack of tribute to the temple that the room is empty and can be made available for Tobiah’s use.

See note on 5:14. Nehemiah returned to the Persian court in 432 B.C.

**king of Babylon.** Some Persian kings used this title after the conquest of the Babylonian Empire (Ezra 5:13), but it was less common by Nehemiah’s day. Its use here may indicate that the king of Persia was then in residence in Babylon.

**I asked leave of the king.** This expression need not imply reappointment as governor, but the actions Nehemiah subsequently takes make it virtually certain that he has resumed his former status.

Cf. Matt. 21:12, 13. Nehemiah allows no compromises and takes immediate remedial action. What has been devoted to the Lord should not be used for personal gain and certainly not to benefit those who are antagonistic to His cause.

While he is clearing Tobiah’s possessions out of the temple, Nehemiah probably asks why such a large storeroom is empty in the first place. It is apparent that the people have lapsed in their giving to maintain the temple ministry.

**13:10 portions of the Levites.** Links this section to the pledge in 10:37. The Levites possess no land (Num. 18:20–24; Deut. 14:29; 18:1), though some may have private income (Deut. 18:8). The dependence of the Levites on the support of the people may explain the reluctance of many Levites to leave Babylonia (Ezra 8:15–20). Lack of support from the people means that the Levites and singers are forced to leave the temple and support themselves by working elsewhere.

See note on 5:7. Nehemiah’s direct action challenges those responsible, not the Levites who left but the temple officials who have permitted such a situation to arise.

**forsaken.** The pledge not to neglect the house of God (10:39) was violated in Nehemiah’s absence.
They do so in keeping with the pledge in 10:37.

See Acts 6:1–5; 2 Cor. 8:16–21. A carefully balanced set of representatives: a priest, a scribe, a Levite, and a layman. Zadok is a short form of the name Zedekiah, probably a reference to the individual named in 10:1.

The fourth use of “remember” in a prayer (1:8 note) and the second of four prayers by Nehemiah with the theme “remember me” (5:19 note).

**my good deeds.** Not a boastful expression but “my acts of covenant loyalty.” Nehemiah is motivated not by self-advancement but by zeal for God’s cause and all that pertains to it.

Sabbath observance was a problem in preexilic times (see Jer. 17:19–27; Amos 8:5). It brought the Lord’s demands on His people’s time into tension with their perception of their economic best interests. The problem seems to have become prevalent during Nehemiah’s absence.

**13:15 Sabbath ... bringing ... sold.** Three links with the pledge in 10:31 that was violated. The people in the countryside were working on the Sabbath to make the most of the grape harvest (late July/September), and they were also bringing produce into Jerusalem on the Sabbath. It is not said they are selling the produce on the holy day; indeed “on the day when they sold food” suggests that Nehemiah’s remonstrance is on a day other than the Sabbath.

These men are one of the “peoples of the land” in view in 10:31. Fish is a significant element in the diet in that day. It is preserved by drying or salting. The Tyrian community in Jerusalem is selling to Jews on the Sabbath.
Again, a direct approach to those responsible for permitting the covenant violations, reminding them of what happened in the past (see Jer. 17:19–27).

The Israelites usually counted days from sunset to sunset (Lev. 23:32; Esth. 4:16; Dan. 8:14 text note). Nehemiah’s direct action extends to closing the entrances of the city to traders from Friday evening. When they do not get the message, he spells out the consequences of further attempts to get around the situation, possibly through setting up a market outside the city wall.

Though he first used members of his entourage to enforce the regulations, Nehemiah now hands the matter over to the proper custodians of this aspect of God’s law for permanent implementation.

**13:22 Remember.** See note on v. 14.

Ezra dealt with the perennial problem of intermarriage in 457 B.C. (Ezra 9:1 note), and in 445 B.C. the people gave solemn commitments regarding it (10:30). It is difficult to see how this problem could arise if Ezra was alive in the preceding decade.

**13:23 Ashdod.** The Persian province between Yehud (Judah) and the Mediterranean; the area of Philistine settlements. See note on 4:7, 8. Their language may be a variant of Aramaic.

It is not just the affront to God involved in such marriages that enrages Nehemiah; it is the corrosive effect on future generations. The problem is not primarily linguistic but concerned the ability of the next generation to hear and learn from the Hebrew Scriptures. The family, which should be the key building block of the covenant community, is being undermined. It is interesting to compare Malachi’s assertion from this period that God seeks godly offspring from the marriages of the covenant community (Mal. 2:15).

Nehemiah’s action can be contrasted with that of Ezra (Ezra 9:3).

**shall not give.** Ezra actually dissolves the illegitimate unions (Ezra 10:3 note), whereas Nehemiah only attempts to prevent such unions in the future through adherence to the terms of their earlier commitment (10:30) and by adding the words “or for yourselves.”

The argument is from the greater to the less: “If Solomon was not spared, how much less will we be spared.” The reference “to sin” pertains to Solomon’s involvement in pagan cults brought to Jerusalem by some of his many wives. The problem is not with foreign women who renounce their gods and pledge fidelity to the Lord, such as Ruth the Moabite (see Ruth 1:16). To be avoided is the insidious influence of a mother committed to worship of the pagan gods.
His marriage is doubly grievous, first, because a high priest in particular is not to marry a foreigner (Lev. 21:14), and second, because Sanballat is an enemy (2:19; 4:1; 6:1).

The sixth use of “remember” in a prayer (1:8 note) and the third imprecatory prayer (4:4, 5 note). Any corruption of the standards of behavior that should prevail in the covenant community is serious, but when the treachery emanates from those responsible for promulgating and maintaining those standards, the situation is doubly shameful and dangerous.

Contributions of wood are made in keeping with the pledge in 10:34, 35.

**Remember me.** See note on v. 14. The book does not end on the high note of 12:27–47 but on the note of failure to carry out the pledges of 10:30–39 and the continuing need for reform. The people of God have not arrived at a resting place. Ezra and Nehemiah show the devotion of the faithful to the temple of God and the community surrounding it, a devotion that comes to maturity in Christ and His church (1 Cor. 3:5–17; Eph. 2:21, 22; 4:16; Heb. 3:1–6).
